source_batch.unit_label: Module A unit 6 (part 1): Theory of Probability: counting, probability rules, random variables, expectation and variance

facts.statement: Probability is a numerical measure of the chance of an event happening, between 0 and 1 (a 60 per cent chance of rain is a probability of 0.6). The factorial of n is n! = n x (n-1) x ... x 2 x 1, with 0! = 1 and 1! = 1.

A permutation is an arrangement in which order matters: P(n, r) = n! / (n - r)! is the number of ways to arrange r of n things. A combination is a selection in which order does not matter: C(n, r) = n! / (r! (n - r)!). The two are related by P(n, r) = r! x C(n, r). Selecting 3 of 5 pencils is C(5, 3) = 10; choosing 3 of 7 boys and 4 of 6 girls can be done in C(7, 3) x C(6, 4) = 35 x 15 = 525 ways.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 106-107, section 6.1 items 1 and 2 and Examples 1 and 2 (the printed note on P and C has a typographical error)

facts.statement: A random experiment has several possible outcomes under identical conditions. The set of all outcomes is the sample space S and its elements are sample points; n(S) is their number. An event is any subset of S. A certain event contains all sample points; an impossible event is the empty set. Events are mutually exclusive if they cannot occur together (A intersect B is empty); equally likely if there is no reason to prefer one; exhaustive if together they make up the sample space (A union B = S); and complementary if they are both exhaustive and mutually exclusive, the complement of A being written A-complement.

If the sample space has n equally likely, exhaustive and mutually exclusive sample points and m of them are favourable to event A, then P(A) = m / n = n(A) / n(S), so 0 <= P(A) <= 1. For two dice n(S) = 36, and the probability that both show the same number is 6/36 = 1/6, that the first shows 6 is 1/6 and that the total is 8 is 5/36. Drawing two balls from a bag of 10 white and 11 black uses combinations: n(S) = C(21, 2) = 210, so P(both white) = C(10, 2)/210 = 45/210 = 0.2143.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 109-111, section 6.2 and Examples 1 to 3

facts.statement: For arrangements, when a pair of items must always be together treat the pair as one item and arrange the group, then arrange the pair internally (six magazines with a given pair together: 5! x 2! = 240 of 6! = 720, probability 1/3); the cases where the pair is never together are the total minus the cases where it is always together (480/720 = 2/3). For a fixed placement such as two named letters at the two ends of six, the remaining letters can be arranged in 4! ways and the two letters in 2! ways, giving 48/720.

Addition theorem: P(A union B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A intersect B). If A and B are mutually exclusive P(A union B) = P(A) + P(B). For three events, P(A union B union C) = P(A) + P(B) + P(C) - P(A int B) - P(B int C) - P(A int C) + P(A int B int C). Also P(A) = P(A int B) + P(A int B-complement), P(A-complement) = 1 - P(A), and the probability of neither event is P(A-complement int B-complement) = 1 - P(A union B). For a card drawn from a pack, P(red or picture) = 26/52 + 12/52 - 6/52 = 8/13.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 112-114, Addition Theorem and corollaries 1 to 7, and Example 1

facts.statement: The conditional probability of A given that B has occurred is P(A | B) = P(A intersect B) / P(B). The multiplication theorem gives P(A int B) = P(A) P(B | A) = P(B) P(A | B). Events are independent if the occurrence of one does not affect the other, and then P(A int B) = P(A) P(B). For two stages, P(B) = P(B | A1) P(A1) + P(B | A2) P(A2). If P(A) = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.4 are independent, P(both) = 0.08, P(only A) = 0.12, P(only B) = 0.32, P(at least one) = 0.52 and P(neither) = 0.48. Odds against an event of 2 to 1 correspond to probability 1/3. If P(A) = 0.8 and P(A int B) = 0.6 then P(B | A) = 0.75.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 113-116, section 6.3 and its examples

facts.statement: A random variable is a function X from the sample space to the real numbers. A discrete random variable takes a finite or countably infinite set of values (age in years, number of arrivals at a clinic, number of accidents); a continuous random variable takes infinitely many values in a range (percentage of marks, weight).

A probability mass function f(x) of a discrete variable satisfies f(x) >= 0 and the sum of f(x) over all x equals 1, with P(X = x) = f(x). A probability density function of a continuous variable satisfies f(x) >= 0 and integrates to 1, and the probability that a continuous variable takes one particular value is zero. The cumulative distribution function is F(x) = P(X <= x); it lies between 0 and 1, is non-decreasing and continuous from the right, with F(minus infinity) = 0 and F(plus infinity) = 1.

The expectation (mean) of a discrete random variable is E(X) = Sum x f(x); the variance is V(X) = E{[X - E(X)]^2} = E(X^2) - (E(X))^2 = Sum (x - E(X))^2 f(x), and the standard deviation is its square root. Properties: E(aX + b) = a E(X) + b and V(aX + b) = a^2 V(X). For f = 0.3, 0.5, 0.2 at x = 1, 2, 3, E(X) = 1.9, E(X^2) = 4.1, V(X) = 0.49, SD = 0.7, and E(2X + 3) = 6.8. If f(0) = k, f(1) = k and f(2) = k + 0.1, then k = 0.3, E(X) = 1.1 and V(X) = 0.69.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 117-119, section 6.6 and Examples 1 and 2

payload.title: Factorials, permutations and combinations
payload.core_explanation_md:
Counting comes before probability. Three tools:

- **n factorial** (n!): multiply n by every whole number below it. By agreement 0! = 1.
- **Permutation** P(n, r): ways to **arrange** r items chosen from n, where order matters (a first, second and third officer in a ranking).
- **Combination** C(n, r): ways to **select** r items from n, where order does not matter (a committee of three).

Every selection of r items can be arranged in r! orders, which is why P(n, r) = r! x C(n, r).

When a task has stages, multiply the ways at each stage: choosing 3 of 7 officers and 4 of 6 clerks gives C(7,3) x C(6,4).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Ask one question: "does swapping two chosen items give a different outcome?" If yes, permutation; if no, combination.

formula_spec.latex_expression: n! = n(n-1)\cdots 1,\quad P(n,r) = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!},\quad C(n,r) = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!},\quad P(n,r) = r!\,C(n,r)
assumptions: Items are distinct and chosen without repetition.
common_errors: Using a permutation when order does not matter.
Adding the ways for different stages instead of multiplying.
Forgetting that C(n, r) = C(n, n - r).

self_check.prompt_text: How many different panels of 3 can be chosen from 8 officers, and how many ways to fill the posts of chair, secretary and treasurer from the same 8?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Panels: C(8,3) = 56. Posts: P(8,3) = 336, which is 3! = 6 times 56.

payload.title: Sample space and events: the vocabulary
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **random experiment** has several possible outcomes, and you cannot say beforehand which will occur: tossing a coin, rolling a die, checking whether a loan will be repaid. List every possible outcome and you have the **sample space** S. An **event** is any collection of outcomes, a subset of S.

| Type of event | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Certain | Contains every outcome |
| Impossible | Contains none (the empty set) |
| Mutually exclusive | Cannot happen together |
| Equally likely | No reason to prefer one outcome |
| Exhaustive | Together they cover the sample space |
| Complementary | Exhaustive **and** mutually exclusive: exactly one of the pair happens |

On one throw of a die, "odd" and "even" are complementary. "Odd" and "multiple of 3" are neither mutually exclusive (3 is both) nor exhaustive (2 is neither).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The complement of A is "A does not happen". Every event and its complement are complementary, so their probabilities add to 1.

self_check.prompt_text: Are "loan approved" and "loan rejected" for one application mutually exclusive, exhaustive, or both?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Both (if no third outcome such as "pending" exists): they cannot happen together and between them cover all outcomes, so they are complementary.

payload.title: Classical probability: favourable over possible
payload.core_explanation_md:
When all outcomes are equally likely, count them:

P(A) = number of outcomes in A divided by number of outcomes in S.

The answer always lies between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).

Counting is where the work is. Use the tools:

- **Selections**: combinations. Two balls from 10 white and 11 black give 210 possible pairs; both white can happen in C(10,2) = 45 ways.
- **Arrangements**: factorials. For "two items always together", glue them into one item, arrange, then arrange inside the glue. For "never together", subtract the "always together" count from the total.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The formula works only if the outcomes you count are equally likely. Counting "heads or tails" outcomes of a biased coin would not give the right probability.

assumptions: Outcomes are equally likely, exhaustive and mutually exclusive.
common_errors: Counting outcomes that are not equally likely.
Using a permutation count for n(A) and a combination count for n(S) (or the reverse).
Reporting a probability above 1.

self_check.prompt_text: Two dice are thrown. What is the probability that the total is 7?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Six of the 36 equally likely outcomes give 7 ((1,6), (2,5), ..., (6,1)), so 6/36 = 1/6.

payload.title: The addition rule and the complement rule
payload.core_explanation_md:
"A **or** B" means at least one of the two happens. Adding P(A) and P(B) counts the overlap twice, so subtract it once:

**P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).**

If A and B are mutually exclusive there is no overlap and the last term is zero.

The **complement rule** is often quicker: P(A does not happen) = 1 - P(A). In particular, P(neither A nor B) = 1 - P(A or B).

For a card drawn from a pack: P(red) = 26/52, P(picture) = 12/52, P(red and picture) = 6/52, so P(red or picture) = 32/52 = 8/13.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: For "at least one" questions, work out the complement ("none") and subtract from 1. It usually saves a lot of arithmetic.

formula_spec.latex_expression: P(A\cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A\cap B),\qquad P(A^c) = 1 - P(A),\qquad P(\text{neither}) = 1 - P(A\cup B)

variables.name: Probability that at least one occurs

assumptions: A and B are events of the same sample space.
For mutually exclusive events P(A and B) = 0.
common_errors: Forgetting to subtract the overlap.
Subtracting the overlap when events are mutually exclusive (it is zero anyway).
Using 1 - P(A) - P(B) for "neither" without removing double counting.

self_check.prompt_text: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A and B) = 0.2. What are P(A or B) and P(neither)?

payload.title: Conditional probability, multiplication and independence
payload.core_explanation_md:
Learning that B has happened changes the odds of A. **Conditional probability** restricts attention to the world where B happened:

P(A given B) = P(A and B) / P(B).

Rearranged, it gives the **multiplication rule**: P(A and B) = P(B) x P(A given B).

If knowing B tells you nothing about A, the events are **independent**, P(A given B) = P(A), and the rule simplifies to P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B).

For a two-stage process, add over the first-stage outcomes (total probability): P(B) = P(B given A1) P(A1) + P(B given A2) P(A2).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Do not confuse independent with mutually exclusive. Two mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are never independent: if one occurs the other certainly does not, so P(A and B) = 0, which differs from P(A) x P(B).

formula_spec.latex_expression: P(A\mid B) = \frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)},\quad P(A\cap B) = P(B)P(A\mid B),\quad \text{independent: } P(A\cap B) = P(A)P(B)

variables.name: Probability of A given that B has occurred

assumptions: Independence is assumed only when the events genuinely do not affect each other.
common_errors: Multiplying P(A) and P(B) for events that are not independent.
Dividing by P(A) instead of P(B) (check which event is "given").
Treating mutually exclusive events as independent.

self_check.prompt_text: P(A) = 0.8 and P(A and B) = 0.6. What is P(B given A)?

payload.title: Putting the rules to work: odds, two stages and independence checks
payload.core_explanation_md:
Three tasks come up often.

**Odds to probability.** Odds of m to n in favour mean probability m/(m+n); odds of m to n against mean probability n/(m+n) in favour. Odds against of 2 to 1 means a probability of 1/3.

**Two stages.** When the second stage depends on the first, split by the first stage and add: P(rejected) = P(rejected given branch A) P(branch A) + P(rejected given branch B) P(branch B).

**Independence check.** Compute P(A) x P(B) and compare with P(A and B). Equal means independent; different means the events influence each other.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Tree diagrams help: each branch carries a conditional probability, multiply along a path, add across paths that lead to the same event.

self_check.prompt_text: Odds against a stock rising are 3 to 2. What is the probability that it rises?

payload.title: Random variables and their distributions
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **random variable** turns an outcome into a number: the number of cheques returned today, the time a customer waits, the return on a portfolio.

| | Discrete | Continuous |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Values | Countable (0, 1, 2, ...) | Any value in a range |
| Example | Accidents, arrivals, age in years | Weight, percentage of marks, waiting time |
| Description of probabilities | **Mass function** f(x): P(X = x) | **Density function** f(x): probability is area under the curve |
| Rule | Each f(x) is at least 0; all f(x) add to 1 | f(x) is at least 0; total area is 1 |

For a continuous variable the probability of any **single exact value** is zero; probabilities belong to intervals.

The **cumulative distribution function** F(x) = P(X is at most x) works for both types. It never decreases, starts at 0 and ends at 1.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A probability table is a valid mass function only if no probability is negative and the probabilities total exactly 1. That is the first check on any distribution you are given.

self_check.prompt_text: A table of probabilities for X = 0, 1, 2 reads 0.5, 0.4, 0.3. Is it a valid distribution?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: the probabilities add to 1.2, not 1.

payload.title: Expectation, variance and standard deviation of a discrete variable
payload.core_explanation_md:
The **expectation** is the long-run average: weight each value by its probability and add.

The **variance** measures scatter about that average: the expected squared deviation. A shortcut is the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean. The **standard deviation** is its square root, back in the original units.

Changing units is easy: adding a constant b shifts the mean by b and leaves the variance unchanged; multiplying by a multiplies the mean by a and the variance by a squared.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: If a payoff is 500 times a count plus a fixed 100, the expected payoff is 500 times the expected count plus 100, and the standard deviation is 500 times that of the count. The fixed 100 does not add any spread.

formula_spec.latex_expression: E(X) = \sum x f(x),\quad V(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2,\quad E(aX+b) = aE(X)+b,\quad V(aX+b) = a^2V(X)
assumptions: The probabilities form a valid distribution (they total 1).
common_errors: Taking E(X squared) as the square of E(X).
Adding b to the variance of aX + b.
Forgetting to square a in V(aX + b).

self_check.prompt_text: E(X) = 21 and V(X) = 49. What are E(2X + 3) and V(3X + 5)?

payload.title: Savings accounts and loans: union, neither, conditional and independence
payload.core_explanation_md: Among a bank's customers, 60 per cent have a savings account (S), 30 per cent have a loan (L) and 20 per cent have both. Find P(S or L), P(neither), P(L given S), and decide whether S and L are independent.

worked_steps.description: Independence test: compare P(S) x P(L) with P(S and L).

payload.final_answer_with_unit: P(S or L) = 0.7; P(neither) = 0.3; P(L given S) = 1/3 (above P(L) = 0.3); not independent, since having a savings account makes a loan slightly more likely

payload.title: Rejection rate across two branches (total probability)
payload.core_explanation_md: Branch A processes 60 per cent of a bank's loan applications and rejects 10 per cent of them; Branch B processes 40 per cent and rejects 20 per cent. What is the probability that a randomly chosen application is rejected?

worked_steps.description: Add the paths that lead to rejection.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Probability of rejection 0.14, that is 14 per cent

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the overall rate not the plain average of 10 and 20 per cent?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The branches handle different shares of the applications, so each rate is weighted by its share (60:40), giving 14 and not 15 per cent.

payload.title: Missing probability, expectation, variance and a linear payoff
payload.core_explanation_md: The number X of overdue instalments on a loan has probabilities 0.4, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1 for X = 0, 1, 2, 3. Find E(X), V(X) and SD, and the mean and standard deviation of the penalty Y = 500X + 100 rupees. Separately, a variable with values 0, 1, 2 has probabilities 2k, 3k and 0.5: find k, E(X), V(X) and the CDF.

worked_steps.description: Second variable: E(X), E(X squared), V(X).

payload.final_answer_with_unit: E(X) = 1, V(X) = 1, SD = 1; penalty mean Rs 600 with standard deviation Rs 500. Second variable: k = 0.1, E = 1.3, V = 0.61, CDF 0.2, 0.5, 1.0

self_check.prompt_text: Why does the fixed Rs 100 not change the standard deviation of the penalty?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Adding a constant shifts every value equally, so the spread about the mean is unchanged; only the multiplier 500 scales it.

items.title: Factorials, permutations and combinations
items.core_explanation_md:
Counting comes before probability. Three tools:

- **n factorial** (n!): multiply n by every whole number below it. By agreement 0! = 1.
- **Permutation** P(n, r): ways to **arrange** r items chosen from n, where order matters (a first, second and third officer in a ranking).
- **Combination** C(n, r): ways to **select** r items from n, where order does not matter (a committee of three).

Every selection of r items can be arranged in r! orders, which is why P(n, r) = r! x C(n, r).

When a task has stages, multiply the ways at each stage: choosing 3 of 7 officers and 4 of 6 clerks gives C(7,3) x C(6,4).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Ask one question: "does swapping two chosen items give a different outcome?" If yes, permutation; if no, combination.

formula_spec.latex_expression: n! = n(n-1)\cdots 1,\quad P(n,r) = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!},\quad C(n,r) = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!},\quad P(n,r) = r!\,C(n,r)
assumptions: Items are distinct and chosen without repetition.
common_errors: Using a permutation when order does not matter.
Adding the ways for different stages instead of multiplying.
Forgetting that C(n, r) = C(n, n - r).

self_check.prompt_text: How many different panels of 3 can be chosen from 8 officers, and how many ways to fill the posts of chair, secretary and treasurer from the same 8?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Panels: C(8,3) = 56. Posts: P(8,3) = 336, which is 3! = 6 times 56.

items.title: Sample space and events: the vocabulary
items.core_explanation_md:
A **random experiment** has several possible outcomes, and you cannot say beforehand which will occur: tossing a coin, rolling a die, checking whether a loan will be repaid. List every possible outcome and you have the **sample space** S. An **event** is any collection of outcomes, a subset of S.

| Type of event | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Certain | Contains every outcome |
| Impossible | Contains none (the empty set) |
| Mutually exclusive | Cannot happen together |
| Equally likely | No reason to prefer one outcome |
| Exhaustive | Together they cover the sample space |
| Complementary | Exhaustive **and** mutually exclusive: exactly one of the pair happens |

On one throw of a die, "odd" and "even" are complementary. "Odd" and "multiple of 3" are neither mutually exclusive (3 is both) nor exhaustive (2 is neither).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The complement of A is "A does not happen". Every event and its complement are complementary, so their probabilities add to 1.

self_check.prompt_text: Are "loan approved" and "loan rejected" for one application mutually exclusive, exhaustive, or both?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Both (if no third outcome such as "pending" exists): they cannot happen together and between them cover all outcomes, so they are complementary.

items.title: Classical probability: favourable over possible
items.core_explanation_md:
When all outcomes are equally likely, count them:

P(A) = number of outcomes in A divided by number of outcomes in S.

The answer always lies between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).

Counting is where the work is. Use the tools:

- **Selections**: combinations. Two balls from 10 white and 11 black give 210 possible pairs; both white can happen in C(10,2) = 45 ways.
- **Arrangements**: factorials. For "two items always together", glue them into one item, arrange, then arrange inside the glue. For "never together", subtract the "always together" count from the total.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The formula works only if the outcomes you count are equally likely. Counting "heads or tails" outcomes of a biased coin would not give the right probability.

assumptions: Outcomes are equally likely, exhaustive and mutually exclusive.
common_errors: Counting outcomes that are not equally likely.
Using a permutation count for n(A) and a combination count for n(S) (or the reverse).
Reporting a probability above 1.

self_check.prompt_text: Two dice are thrown. What is the probability that the total is 7?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Six of the 36 equally likely outcomes give 7 ((1,6), (2,5), ..., (6,1)), so 6/36 = 1/6.

items.title: The addition rule and the complement rule
items.core_explanation_md:
"A **or** B" means at least one of the two happens. Adding P(A) and P(B) counts the overlap twice, so subtract it once:

**P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).**

If A and B are mutually exclusive there is no overlap and the last term is zero.

The **complement rule** is often quicker: P(A does not happen) = 1 - P(A). In particular, P(neither A nor B) = 1 - P(A or B).

For a card drawn from a pack: P(red) = 26/52, P(picture) = 12/52, P(red and picture) = 6/52, so P(red or picture) = 32/52 = 8/13.
items.expanded_explanation_md: For "at least one" questions, work out the complement ("none") and subtract from 1. It usually saves a lot of arithmetic.

formula_spec.latex_expression: P(A\cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A\cap B),\qquad P(A^c) = 1 - P(A),\qquad P(\text{neither}) = 1 - P(A\cup B)

variables.name: Probability that at least one occurs

assumptions: A and B are events of the same sample space.
For mutually exclusive events P(A and B) = 0.
common_errors: Forgetting to subtract the overlap.
Subtracting the overlap when events are mutually exclusive (it is zero anyway).
Using 1 - P(A) - P(B) for "neither" without removing double counting.

items.title: Conditional probability, multiplication and independence
items.core_explanation_md:
Learning that B has happened changes the odds of A. **Conditional probability** restricts attention to the world where B happened:

P(A given B) = P(A and B) / P(B).

Rearranged, it gives the **multiplication rule**: P(A and B) = P(B) x P(A given B).

If knowing B tells you nothing about A, the events are **independent**, P(A given B) = P(A), and the rule simplifies to P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B).

For a two-stage process, add over the first-stage outcomes (total probability): P(B) = P(B given A1) P(A1) + P(B given A2) P(A2).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Do not confuse independent with mutually exclusive. Two mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are never independent: if one occurs the other certainly does not, so P(A and B) = 0, which differs from P(A) x P(B).

formula_spec.latex_expression: P(A\mid B) = \frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)},\quad P(A\cap B) = P(B)P(A\mid B),\quad \text{independent: } P(A\cap B) = P(A)P(B)

variables.name: Probability of A given that B has occurred

assumptions: Independence is assumed only when the events genuinely do not affect each other.
common_errors: Multiplying P(A) and P(B) for events that are not independent.
Dividing by P(A) instead of P(B) (check which event is "given").
Treating mutually exclusive events as independent.

items.title: Putting the rules to work: odds, two stages and independence checks
items.core_explanation_md:
Three tasks come up often.

**Odds to probability.** Odds of m to n in favour mean probability m/(m+n); odds of m to n against mean probability n/(m+n) in favour. Odds against of 2 to 1 means a probability of 1/3.

**Two stages.** When the second stage depends on the first, split by the first stage and add: P(rejected) = P(rejected given branch A) P(branch A) + P(rejected given branch B) P(branch B).

**Independence check.** Compute P(A) x P(B) and compare with P(A and B). Equal means independent; different means the events influence each other.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Tree diagrams help: each branch carries a conditional probability, multiply along a path, add across paths that lead to the same event.

self_check.prompt_text: Odds against a stock rising are 3 to 2. What is the probability that it rises?

items.title: Random variables and their distributions
items.core_explanation_md:
A **random variable** turns an outcome into a number: the number of cheques returned today, the time a customer waits, the return on a portfolio.

| | Discrete | Continuous |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Values | Countable (0, 1, 2, ...) | Any value in a range |
| Example | Accidents, arrivals, age in years | Weight, percentage of marks, waiting time |
| Description of probabilities | **Mass function** f(x): P(X = x) | **Density function** f(x): probability is area under the curve |
| Rule | Each f(x) is at least 0; all f(x) add to 1 | f(x) is at least 0; total area is 1 |

For a continuous variable the probability of any **single exact value** is zero; probabilities belong to intervals.

The **cumulative distribution function** F(x) = P(X is at most x) works for both types. It never decreases, starts at 0 and ends at 1.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A probability table is a valid mass function only if no probability is negative and the probabilities total exactly 1. That is the first check on any distribution you are given.

self_check.prompt_text: A table of probabilities for X = 0, 1, 2 reads 0.5, 0.4, 0.3. Is it a valid distribution?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: the probabilities add to 1.2, not 1.

items.title: Expectation, variance and standard deviation of a discrete variable
items.core_explanation_md:
The **expectation** is the long-run average: weight each value by its probability and add.

The **variance** measures scatter about that average: the expected squared deviation. A shortcut is the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean. The **standard deviation** is its square root, back in the original units.

Changing units is easy: adding a constant b shifts the mean by b and leaves the variance unchanged; multiplying by a multiplies the mean by a and the variance by a squared.
items.expanded_explanation_md: If a payoff is 500 times a count plus a fixed 100, the expected payoff is 500 times the expected count plus 100, and the standard deviation is 500 times that of the count. The fixed 100 does not add any spread.

formula_spec.latex_expression: E(X) = \sum x f(x),\quad V(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2,\quad E(aX+b) = aE(X)+b,\quad V(aX+b) = a^2V(X)
assumptions: The probabilities form a valid distribution (they total 1).
common_errors: Taking E(X squared) as the square of E(X).
Adding b to the variance of aX + b.
Forgetting to square a in V(aX + b).

items.stem_md: Two dice are thrown. What is the probability that the total is 7? (Give the decimal to 4 places.)

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 4 decimal places.

items.correct_explanation_md: Six of the 36 outcomes give a total of 7, so the probability is 6/36 = 0.1667.

items.stem_md: Three fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting at least one head?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 3 decimal places.

items.correct_explanation_md: There are 8 equally likely outcomes and only TTT has no head, so P = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8 = 0.875.

items.stem_md: The odds against a stock price rising are 3 to 2. What is the probability that it rises?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

items.correct_explanation_md: Odds against 3 to 2 mean 3 parts against and 2 parts for, so P(rise) = 2/5 = 0.40.

worked_solution_steps.description: Parts in favour over total parts.
